conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having a lot of abdominal pain and vomiting again. Can you tell me what’s been going on since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was still in pain when I left last time. I’ve had burning in my stomach and I’ve thrown up a few times—some looked like coffee grounds again. I just can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you have any other symptoms—like dizziness, fever, or changes in your bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt really lightheaded yesterday while walking—I told people I was going to pass out, and I did. I was out for about 40 seconds. No injury, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. We’ll look into that. You’ve also had chronic pancreatitis pain—does this feel like that, or different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s both. The burning is new, but the pain in my back—that’s my usual pancreatitis flare. I just can’t handle it without my IV Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand the pain is real. But we need to be careful with IV narcotics. We’ll manage your pain, but we also want to avoid complications. You’re on prednisone—could that be making the stomach burning worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think so. My doctor said it could cause gastritis. But I need the steroids for my Sjogren’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re continuing that. But we’re also starting you on omeprazole twice daily to protect your stomach. We’ve ordered a CT scan to check for any new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But please, I need my Dilaudid—I get anxious when I don’t have it scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you 6 mg IV in the ER already. We’ll reassess your pain and adjust as needed. For now, we’re keeping you NPO—nothing by mouth except meds—so your stomach can rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan came back. It didn’t show any blockages, inflammation, or bleeding sources. But there’s a slight narrowing at the end of your stomach—could be contributing to the vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my endoscopy was normal last time. Doesn’t that rule out ulcers or bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we repeated it—still normal. No ulcers, no varices. But you are positive for H. pylori, which can cause gastritis even without visible ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that could be why I’m vomiting blood? But I’ve had H. pylori for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be flaring now, especially with the prednisone. We’ll start you on antibiotics once you can tolerate oral meds. For now, we’re keeping you on IV fluids and omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I at least have my Dilaudid? I’m in pain and I’m scared it’ll get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working with the pain team. They suggest switching to Dilaudid suppositories—they’ve helped you before when you couldn’t take pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess… but I really want the IV. Why don’t you believe me when I say how bad it is?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We do believe you. Your pain is real. But we need to find a safe way to manage it long-term. The suppositories are effective and reduce the risk of dependency. We’ll try one now and see how you respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling? Any nausea or pain since the suppository?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The pain’s down. But I’m still scared to eat. What if I vomit again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll start you on clear liquids slowly. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet. We’re also adding a stool softener—narcotics can cause constipation, which might worsen pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about the fainting? I’ve never passed out before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your POTS, it’s likely related to low blood pressure when standing, especially with dehydration from vomiting. We’re keeping you on IV fluids and continuing fludrocortisone. You haven’t had any more episodes, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t taken midodrine at home—it makes me jittery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. We’ll stick with fludrocortisone and hydration. The key is gradual movement and small, frequent meals once you’re eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable—no anemia, kidney function is normal. We’d like to start your H. pylori treatment today: amoxicillin and clarithromycin for 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help the vomiting? And can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should reduce stomach inflammation over time. You’re doing much better—tolerating liquids, pain controlled with suppositories. If you keep this up, we can discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about managing pain at home. What if I need more Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with 10 suppositories—3 mg every 3 hours as needed. Also, Tylenol suppositories for backup. And we’ve increased your escitalopram to help with both anxiety and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment with my psychiatrist next week. Should I switch to Cymbalta?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team recommends discussing Cymbalta with your psychopharmacist. It can help with nerve pain and mood. We’ve included the recommendation in your discharge summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great today—eating soft foods, no vomiting, pain well-controlled. We’re planning discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m still worried about the fainting. Should I avoid standing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, just rise slowly. Keep hydrated, eat small meals, and continue fludrocortisone. If dizziness returns, sit down and call your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary. You’ll continue omeprazole twice daily, finish the antibiotics, and use the suppositories as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll follow up with my GI and rheumatologist about switching from prednisone to methotrexate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That should help reduce steroid-related gastritis. Call your doctor if pain worsens, you can’t keep food down, or you feel dizzy. Otherwise, take it slow and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to hear that. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if you need help.
